title: The tin can was invented about 45 years before the can opener
body: Peter Durand obtained an English patent for preserving food in tin cans in 1810, and Bryan Donkin bought it in 1812 and began canning. The first cans were robust containers that weighed more than the food inside, and the instructions read **cut round the top near the outer edge with a chisel and hammer**. Nobody patented a tool for the job until Robert Yeates’s claw-ended opener in England in 1855 and Ezra Warner’s lever opener in the United States in 1858. The familiar cutting wheel arrived in 1870, from William Lyman of Meriden, Connecticut.

slides.heading: Why the wait?
slides.text: The first cans were heavy containers that weighed more than their contents, and the tools people already owned did the job, so nobody saw the point of developing a new one. Can walls grew thinner, yet a general-purpose opener still took decades.

slides.prompt: In 1865 a tin of ‘Bully beef’ came with its own opener. What was it called?
slides.detail: A home-use opener designed in 1865 and supplied with cans of pickled beef named Bully beef.

slides.heading: Oldest first
slides.explanation: Can 1810, Donkin 1812, Yeates 1855, Warner 1858, and Lyman’s rotating wheel in 1870.
